problem: Multi-target RL agents that must reach an instructed goal among several objects learn goal identity only implicitly from sparse rewards, so they are sample-inefficient and generalize poorly to visually complex, unseen backgrounds. Prior auxiliary losses (VAE, contrastive, reward prediction) model the whole environment rather than the goal states.
motivation: Realistic robots must interact with many possible targets given instructions, so agents need to discriminate targets semantically. Goal states are rare but highly informative, and the environment supplies their labels for free through the instruction and episode success.
key_idea: Auto-label the goal states reached in successful episodes, train a goal-discriminator on them with a cross-entropy auxiliary loss (GACE), and use its hidden features as an attention query (GDAN) to focus the policy on goal-relevant information.
insight: Learning representations only from goal states is more effective than learning them from all states: it beats VAE and RAD on sample efficiency and on unseen backgrounds (V2 unseen 76.36 vs 19.79 for VAE). Freezing the discriminator early (10K/20K updates) slows learning compared with the unfrozen version, so the auxiliary loss itself drives the gain. Naively concatenating the discriminator features gives 81.5% on R1 vs 89.3% with attention, so attention is what filters out the noise from sparse goal information. Saliency maps show that A3C fixates on background edges, while GACE&GDAN attends to the goal only.
method: Auto-labeled goal states: when an episode ends at the goal, the tuple (goal state, one_hot(goal)) is stored. Failed-episode states are stored as a negative class with probability eps_N, and a random-policy warmup fills the buffer first.

GACE loss: the shared feature extractor sigma feeds an MLP goal-discriminator d (256 units, then N outputs). It is trained with cross-entropy on the stored goal states, and L_total = L_RL + eta*L_GACE with eta=0.5. The discriminator is only used in training, except that its first layer supplies the GDAN query.

GDAN attention: the query q comes from the first linear layer of the discriminator applied to e_t. Key and value come from gated-attention (instruction-gated) features passed through an LSTM (a linear layer for manipulation) and split in half. u = tanh(Wq q + Wk k) and h = v ⊙ u, and h is concatenated with the gated-attention state features to compute policy and value.
Base RL: A3C with gated-attention plus LSTM for ViZDoom navigation; deterministic Pixel-SAC (no LSTM) for UR5 manipulation.
Sample-efficiency metrics: SRR = n_B/n_A and SEI = (n_A-n_B)/n_B, measured by the number of updates needed to reach a reference success ratio set by a baseline.
Benchmarks: ViZDoom V1-V4 (fixed or shuffled positions, maze, random background textures with seen/unseen splits) and MuJoCo UR5 R1-R3 (random checkered backgrounds, 5 target classes).

setting.backbone: CNN feature extractor (4 conv layers) + gated-attention + LSTM ActorCritic + MLP goal-discriminator, trained from scratch with A3C (navigation) / SAC (manipulation)
setting.training_data: online RL interaction only, plus self-collected auto-labeled goal states (goal storage of 500K in manipulation); no external data
setting.observation: ViZDoom: 42x42 RGB-D, 4 stacked frames; UR5: 84x84 RGB third-person camera; a discrete goal instruction
setting.action_space: ViZDoom: discrete MoveForward/TurnLeft/TurnRight; UR5: continuous joint control
setting.privileged: none (goal labels come from the instruction and episode success signal; the number of target classes is assumed known)

numbers.extra: trained on the same environment; random-policy SR is 6.6%

numbers_note: Custom benchmarks only; no standard embodied-navigation benchmarks. Learning curves are given in figures. Also reported: SEI 1702.94% (V1, vs A3C) and 398.57% (R1).
results: GACE&GDAN beats A3C, +VAE and +RAD on all ViZDoom tasks (V3 78.21 vs 33.45 for A3C; V2 unseen 76.36 vs 19.79 for VAE). It also beats SAC, +AE and +CURL on UR5 tasks (R1 89.3 vs 67.9 for CURL). It reaches the reference success ratio with far fewer updates: SEI is 1702.94% in V1 and 485.41% in R1 (GACE alone).
limitations: Requires an explicit instruction that names a target and a known, fixed number of target classes; it is not applicable to tasks with unspecified targets or with little correlation between state and reward.
Evaluated only on custom, simple simulated benchmarks (ViZDoom, MuJoCo) with a small number of target classes, and not on standard photorealistic navigation benchmarks or real robots.
On the easier R1 task GACE alone is more sample-efficient than GACE&GDAN, and gains depend on how similar goal states are to other states.
